results.title: Incorporating additional evidence as prior information to resolve non-identifiability in Bayesian disease model calibration. A tutorial.
results.content:
Title: Incorporating additional evidence as prior information to resolve non-identifiability in Bayesian disease model calibration. A tutorial.
# Incorporating additional evidence as prior information to resolve non-identifiability in Bayesian disease model calibration. The question of non-identifiability poses a challenge to disease model calibration where multiple parameter sets generate identical model outputs. Through case studies, we demonstrate how informative priors can help resolve non-identifiability and improve model inference. A model is said to be *non-identifiable* if two or more distinct sets of parameter values can produce the same observed data. We will demonstrate that by doing this, researchers can obtain reliable parameter estimates for their disease models, even in the presence of non-identifiability. Non-identifiability can lead to wide credible intervals or flat posterior distributions, making it difficult to draw precise inferences about model parameters. To address the challenges of non-identifiability, this tutorial focuses on incorporating informative prior distributions for model parameters. This approach is supported by the work of Neath and Samaniego [38], who demonstrated the effectiveness of prior information in handling a non-identifiable model. By effectively incorporating prior information, we can improve the precision and reliability of parameter estimates in SIS models, especially when dealing with non-identifiability issues. To address non-identifiability in models, prior information can be invaluable. To incorporate prior information into the SIS model, we can specify a prior distribution for the transmission rate (β𝛽\betaitalic\_β). By carefully incorporating prior information, we can enhance the reliability and interpretability of disease models, even in the presence of non-identifiability. By carefully selecting Gamma parameters based on expert knowledge and available data, we were able to incorporate valuable prior information into our model, enhancing the reliability of our parameter estimates and improving the overall robustness of our HPV model calibration. Even though there was not enough information in the data and the model itself to identify good parameter values, and the prior on this parameter was vague, there was enough information in other parameter’s priors to have a knock-on effect and for the posterior distribution to have a pronounced peak, especially for CIN23 to Local Cancer (HR 16). By incorporating informative priors, we were able to effectively address the challenges of non-identifiability and improve the precision of our parameter estimates.

results.title: How to determine identifiability of parameters under uncertainty? - Questions - PyMC Discourse
results.content:
Title: How to determine identifiability of parameters under uncertainty? - Questions - PyMC Discourse
# How to determine identifiability of parameters under uncertainty? Does anybody knows how to determine if a parameter of model is identifiable (or not), with pymc3??? I don’t think there is an automatic way to identify identifiablity issues. I found in this paper link to paper, deterministic ways to determine the un-identifiability of parameters (going from Fisher’s matrix to profile likelihood). I was wondering if there is something similar for the case of “noisy-random” observed data. It was an interesting practical take on identifiability issues, which I wasn’t aware of. Some model misspecification / departures from the likelihood function? One thing that makes identifiability analysis less straightforward in a Bayesian setting is that the distinction between latent and observed variables is not as clear as in MLE. Two parameters that are jointly unidentifiable in MLE maybe identifiable in a Bayesian setting if given precise enough priors. I found a very vague discussion here in relation to Bayesian models:. I referred to “noisy/random” data as a justification to use Bayesian inversion… If the observed data is deterministic (error-free) and the model to fit is also deterministic, then you can use least squares and that’s the end of the problem, at first sight. When the observed data, has a level of noise, the least-squares is replaced by Bayesianism and instead of obtaining a “unique” tuple that minimizes the “residual definition” you obtain a probability that maximizes the likelihood functions. Anyway, there is a lot of literature in the field of identifiability for deterministic models and fittings, but I couldn’t find the equivalent for Bayesian inversion. | Observed Deterministic  Questions | 12 | 9960 | June 19, 2022 |. | Identifiable up to rearrangement  Questions | 7 | 964 | May 29, 2019 |. | Problem with Deterministic variable  Questions | 7 | 1082 | March 22, 2021 |. | Should I add pm.Deterministic to my model? modeling | 6 | 771 | June 6, 2024 |. | Building a normal likelihood with known but varying variance for every data point/sample  Questions | 1 | 429 | February 20, 2021 |.

results.title: Bayesian calibration of computer models based on Takagi–Sugeno fuzzy models - ScienceDirect
results.content:
Title: Bayesian calibration of computer models based on Takagi–Sugeno fuzzy models - ScienceDirect
A new Bayesian calibration framework of computer models based on Takagi–Sugeno fuzzy model is developed. Further, based on the T–S fuzzy model prior for the model discrepancy function, we construct the Bayesian model for the calibration problem and design a sampler which combines Gibbs and Metropolis–Hastings steps, forming the framework of Bayesian calibration method based on Takagi–Sugeno fuzzy model (BC-TS). Model calibration, or model updating [2], is the process of estimating the unknown model parameters and simultaneously determining the model discrepancy function by comparing the system responses from simulation predictions and real observations. The classical Bayesian calibration method uses a Gaussian process as the formula form of the model discrepancy function, which actually is a prior assumption of smoothness of the input–output relation [14]. To our best knowledge, most existing calibration frameworks treat the model discrepancy function as a black-box model and estimate its parameters together with the calibration parameters based on the experimental data. In addition to focusing on formulating prior information about the model discrepancy, this paper also addresses the identifiability issue of the Bayesian calibration method. By bringing a T–S fuzzy model into the Bayesian framework of model calibration, we are intended to exploit the expert knowledge to construct an informative prior for the model discrepancy so that high-level identifiability can be achieved and an interpretable model can be obtained. Second, a novel framework of Bayesian calibration based on Takagi–Sugeno fuzzy model (BC-TS) is proposed. ## Bayesian calibration based on Takagi–Sugeno fuzzy model. This section introduces the proposed Bayesian calibration approach based on Takagi–Sugeno fuzzy model (BC-TS). This paper proposes a novel framework for the calibration of computer models, i.e., Bayesian calibration based on Takagi–Sugeno (T–S) fuzzy model (BC-TS). A Bayesian calibration based on Takagi–Sugeno fuzzy model (BC-TS) is applied to identify the exactly parameters of the FCT’s reaction wheel model in this subsection. [16] proposed a novel sequential calibration and validation approach based on the KOH framework to mitigate the effects of prior distributions of model parameters on the calibration results. [17] proposed a Bayesian calibration framework based on the Takagi–Sugeno fuzzy model to conveniently exploit expert knowledge to construct informative priors for the model discrepancy.
